thread.title: Underwater Umbrellas Reduce Coral Bleaching in Caribbean Test
thread.title_full: Underwater Umbrellas Reduce Coral Bleaching in Caribbean Test

author: HeadTopics.com
title: Underwater Umbrellas Reduce Coral Bleaching in Caribbean Test
text:
Researchers tested underwater umbrellas in the Caribbean and found they reduced coral bleaching by 60% light exposure, offering a simple tool to protect reefs.
Scientists have tested simple underwater umbrellas that shade corals and found they reduce bleaching in the Caribbean, according to a study published today in Frontiers in Marine Science. The research, led by Karen Neely of Nova Southeastern University, was conducted at Newfound Harbor in the Florida Keys during the summer of 2024.
Underwater Umbrellas Tested in Florida Keys
The shades, made of pipes with nylon cloths attached, are fixed to the seabed and float about a foot (30 centimeters) above a coral. Neely and her colleagues set up 20 shades over 10 different colonies of two species of brain coral. They also picked 20 matching corals that would remain unshaded to serve as controls. The shades reduced corals' light exposure by 60%. Donning scuba gear, the researchers visited the corals every two weeks to look for color changes and biopsy their tissues.
They then analyzed those tissue samples in the lab to monitor the algae living inside. That summer, the heat stress measured at Newfound Harbor was the second-highest on record, but the shaded corals suffered less bleaching than expected. The biggest differences were noticed during the most intense periods of heat stress. The shades also appeared to reverse bleaching that had already occurred, as some of the corals started to get their color back.
Interestingly, the unshaded corals also saw less bleaching than expected, and none of the corals in either group died. Neely and her colleagues suspect that may be because the marine heatwave caused most of the corals to be occupied by an algae called Durusdinium trenchii. This species is particularly heat tolerant but is associated with reduced coral growth and perhaps greater susceptibility to disease.
What is more, the researchers did not observe any differences in density of algae occupation or algae species between the shaded and unshaded corals. That may have been due to the fact that their permits stipulated sampling from the corals' edges, which are less exposed to sunlight and experience less bleaching. They also believe the shades might have been more effective if they had installed them before water temperatures rose high enough to cause bleaching.
Despite these caveats, the shades still had a measurable positive impact, and Neely said her team did not see any evidence to suggest that they caused harm to other parts of the ecosystem. The experiment serves as a proof-of-concept for positive shading effects on Caribbean corals, and future designs could work for larger reef areas. Next, she hopes to investigate the longer-term effects these shades have on corals. Theoretically they should reduce subsequent disease and increase subsequent reproduction, but this needs to be tested, she said.
Coral Bleaching Threat and Global Warming
Coral bleaching occurs when corals expel the symbiotic algae that live in their tissues. These algae, called zooxanthellae, give corals their signature bright colors and also serve as their primary food source. Without zooxanthellae, corals turn white, hence the term bleaching, and begin to starve.
Scientists expect that by 2050, the world's oceans will have warmed so much that most reefs suffer mass bleaching every year. The decimation of these vital ecosystems threatens numerous other marine species, natural protections for coastal communities, and the multi-billion dollar fishing industry that feeds and employs millions of people. Cooling the waters that corals live in will require global action. Humanity will need to cut its greenhouse gas emissions to net-zero and remove carbon from the atmosphere to reverse the current warming trend.
Until we can achieve those feats, scientists are developing strategies to mitigate the damage to coral reefs. Shading has emerged as one promising solution, and researchers have conducted experiments in the Pacific Ocean using a variety of designs, according to Neely. Her team's design was inspired by a colleague in Dominica who created a few of the umbrella-like structures during the marine heatwave of 2023.
Neely said the particular structures they deployed are good for smaller areas, like individual high-priority corals, coral nurseries, or small outplant areas, but new engineering ideas could make it suitable for larger reef areas.
Future Research and Broader Implications
As Earth's oceans continue to warm, scientists are racing to find ways to protect coral reefs. The underwater umbrellas offer a simple, low-cost method that could be scaled up with further engineering. Neely hopes to investigate the longer-term effects these shades have on corals, such as reducing disease and increasing reproduction.
The study's findings are a hopeful sign that shading could help corals survive the coming decades. However, without drastic cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, coral reefs may still face extinction. The research serves as a reminder that while local interventions can help, global action on climate change remains essential.
